Analysis: Both hypotheses present innovative approaches integrating genetic predisposition, alcohol-induced gut dysbiosis, and subsequent inflammatory signaling in the progression of liver disease to HCC. Hypothesis 1 is novel in its detailed linking of acetaldehyde and ROS production with disruptions in lipid metabolism and its emphasis on advanced experimental tools like gut‐on‐a‐chip systems and engineered probiotics. However, its complexity may present challenges in mechanistic clarity and quantifiable endpoints. Hypothesis 2, while similarly novel, offers a slightly more streamlined model by clearly identifying specific microbial shifts (loss of butyrate producers and gain of LPS producers) along with a defined IL-6/STAT3 inflammatory pathway. This clarity improves its plausibility and testability, as it provides concrete targets for multi-omics and intervention studies. Both are relatively safe, though the translational interventions (engineered probiotics versus FMT or precision probiotics) carry similar emerging safety considerations. Overall, given its focused mechanistic pathway and clearer experimental endpoints, Hypothesis 2 stands out as the more robust and testable option.
